newsitem.title: UK: British bank consolidation -- smoke without fire?.
newsitem.headline: British bank consolidation -- smoke without fire?.

text.p: If British newspapers and market rumours are to be believed, British banks are engaged in a constant round of takeover manoeuvres -- but this has so far produced much smoke but little fire.
While international investment banking continues to consolidate, however, Britain's retail banking and financial services industry could also see more major activity, analysts said on Monday.
A major banking merger has not been pulled off here since 1995, when Lloyds merged with TSB.
But despite the complexity of such deals, many analysts see more on the horizon in a sector where share prices have romped ahead this year.
"We're looking at a situation where the economics of further consolidation is pretty compelling," said Salomon Brothers banking analyst John Leonard on Monday.

The British banking industry has seen three new entrants so far this year, led by the country's premier mortgage lender Halifax Plc and joined on Monday by Woolwich Plc which immediately started trading with a takeover/merger premium.

The new entrants, which also include Alliance & Leicester, all have excess capital and none would present a problem in terms of market share for monopolies watchdogs if they were to be seen as merger partners.

Alliance and Woolwich both have five-year protection against takeover, but this would be lost if they made a move on another financial institution or if 75 percent of their shareholders waived it, which would be likely if the directors were to recommend a merger.
The recent spate of takeover talk was sparked by National Westminster Bank when news it had approached former building society Abbey National was leaked.

NatWest, having problems at its investment banking unit NatWest Markets, was immediately deemed to have put itself in play and since then has been linked with pretty well any feasible and many unfeasible merger partners.
Perhaps the most startling of these prospects has been the linking of NatWest to its fellow big-league player Barclays Plc.

The biggest block to this scenario seems to be the massive market share the combination would have in the small and medium sized business banking sector -- at least fifty percent -- and the massive job reductions -- possibly as many as 40,000 -- which would be needed to make the deal economic.
Few analysts see the new Labour Party government allowing such a prospect.
But should such British considerations stop such mergers when viewed in an international context?

Many analysts see large cross-border mergers in the future aided by a common European currency, but in Britain, there are other factors which make further consolidation of the financial services industry possible.

New methods of product distribution -- supermarket banking and the internet, for example -- mean companies are always looking for opportunities to leverage either their product base or their distribution capabilities.
This means, according to UBS banking analyst John Aitken, that the most likely links could be between banks and life assurance companies.

Insurance companies such as Prudential Corp Plc have been linked with banks but analysts are unsure what they would bring to the party apart from large capital and in the Pru's case a massive fund management business.

That may apply to a bank like NatWest which has a broad range, but for Halifax, with a big bias towards mortgage and savings business, a link to a firm offering pensions products must be the way ahead.
Aitken is not convinced of the basic case for banking consolidation, however, pointing out that British banks are making good returns.
"If the market were truly over-banked then profitability ought to be lower," Aitken said. "The case is far from clear cut."
Aitken sees national consolidation being given a spur by the introduction of a comon currency as smaller players get squeezed, and expects this to move in tandem with international merger activity
